fetched_contents.text: Immobilized-metal affinity chromatography adsorbent with paramagnetism and its application in purification of histidine-tagged proteins Abstract A new method for synthesis of an Immobilized-Metal Affinity chromatography (IMAC) adsorbent with superparamagnetism (Fe3O4/SiO2-GPTMS-Asp-Co) was reported in this paper. Fe3O4 nanoparticles were first modified by SiO2 to form the core–shell Fe3O4/SiO2 with superparamagnetism, the core–shell microspheres were then successively treated by 3-glycidoxypropyltrimethoxysilane (GPTMS), l-aspartic acid (l-Asp) and 2-bromoacetic acid to form Fe3O4/SiO2-GPTMS-Asp nanoparticles with tetradentate ligands. Finally, the IMAC adsorbent with superparamagnetism, Fe3O4/SiO2-GPTMS-Asp-Co, was finally obtained by the coordination of Co2+ with the resulting nanoparticles. The intermediates and product obtained from the process mentioned above were characterized by TEM, SEM, XRD, XPS, FT-IR, TGA, AAS, EDS, element analysis and magnetic hysteresis loop. Fe3O4/SiO2-GPTMS-Asp-Co nanoparticles used as IMAC adsorbent to separate the recombinant 6-histidine-tagged gp41 protein were investigated. The result indicates that the IMAC adsorbent we prepared has outstanding advantages in the separation of the 6-histidine-tagged proteins from the crude bacterial lysate, such as simple operation, high selectivity and capacity. Introduction Immobilized-metal affinity chromatography (IMAC) is a separation technique that uses covalently bound chelating compounds on solid chromatographic supports to entrap metal ions, which serve as affinity ligands for various proteins, making use of coordinative binding of some amino acid residues exposed on the surface. This separation technique is used rapid purification and substantial purity of the product [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6]. Everson and Parker firstly used immobilization of chelating compounds to the separation of metalloproteinase [7]. IMAC technique became popular through the research work of Porath [8], [9], [10] and Sulkowski [2], [11], [12] who laid the foundations of the technique that is widely used today and applicable for a variety of purposes, including analytical and preparative purification of proteins, as well as being a valuable tool for studying surface accessibility of certain amino acid residues. IMAC techniques were initially used for separating proteins and peptides with natural histidine residues. The work of Hochuli et al. [13] pioneered the efficient purification of recombinant proteins with engineered histidine affinity handles attached to the N- or C-terminus, especially in combination with the Ni(II)–nitrilotriacetic acid (Ni–NTA) matrix, which selectively binds adjacent histamines. An ideal affinity tag should enable effective but not too strong a binding, and allow elution of the desired protein under mild, nondestructive conditions. In the common chelating ligands, because of the 3-dentation, the binding force of iminodiacetic acid (IDA) with the metal ion is weak. However, the 5-dentation, the complex between metal ion and tris(carboxymethyl)ethylenediamine (TED) has only one bond to act with the 6-histidine-tagged proteins, which makes the binding force of the protein with the complex too weak [14]. The tetradentate NTA bind the metal ion with an extra carboxylate oxygen compared with IDA, this could give it a superior metal chelating strength, and the complex of NTA with the metal ion has two bonds to act with the 6-histidine-tagged proteins, which makes a stronger protein retention power compared with TED [5]. So, tetradentate ligand is relatively suitable to be a ligand immobilized on IMAC for purification of the 6-histidine-tagged proteins. The core–shell nano- or microparticles with superparamagnetism are widely applied in biomedical and diagnostic fields, including separation of biochemical products [15], enzyme encapsulation [16], immunoassay [17], and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) [18]. Based on these researches, some materials combining IMAC and superparamagnetism used in protein separation have been developed in the past decades. Especially, magnetic IMAC adsorbent with nano size were extremely concerned because (1) their high surface/volume ratio and good solubility result in a higher binding rate, (2) their nanometer sizes lead to faster movement and easy entry into cells, and (3) their magnetically controllable aggregation behavior allows them to be anchored onto a solid support for further usage. Today, some commercially magnetic IMAC adsorbents have been appeared, such as Ferromagnetic Dynabeads M-280 (Dynal, Lake Success) [19], BioMag superparamagnetic particles (Perspective Diagnostics, Cambridge, MA) [20] and IDA–Cu(II) or IDA–Zn(II) magnetic agarose [21]. Although some commercially magnetic IMAC adsorbents have been used in application, improvement of magnetic IMAC adsorbents performance is also required. Bong et al. [22] described the development of functionalized magnetic nanoparticles (MNPs) with PEG-modification, a phospholipids micelle coating, and their use in manipulating histidine-tagged proteins. Due to their high surface/volume ratio, the MNPs showed better performance (about 100 times higher) in immobilizing engineered proteins than conventional micrometer-sized beads. Thomas et al. [23] developed a novel nickel–silica matrix for the generation of magnetic beads for metal-ion affinity chromatography. In contrast to magnetic Ni–NTA agarose beads, the novel particle type consists of a magnetic core and a nickel–silica composite matrix with the nickel ions tightly integrated in the silica. With the SiMAC beads, greatly improved purification of histidine-tagged proteins from crude bacterial extracts was achieved. The yield was at least twice as high as that obtained by using conventional materials. A similar result has been recently obtained [24]. Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2024 Jul 1. Published in final edited form as: Anal Bioanal Chem. 2023 Apr 5;415(18):4521–4531. doi: 10.1007/s00216-023-04677-9 Abstract Protein phosphorylation is a vital and common post-translational modification (PTM) in cells, modulating various biological processes and diseases. Comprehensive top-down proteomics of phosphorylated proteoforms (phosphoproteoforms) in cells and tissues is essential for a better understanding of the roles of protein phosphorylation in fundamental biological processes and diseases. Mass spectrometry (MS)–based top-down proteomics of phosphoproteoforms remains challenging due to their relatively low abundance. Herein, we investigated magnetic nanoparticle–based immobilized metal affinity chromatography (IMAC, Ti4+, and Fe3+) for selective enrichment of phosphoproteoforms for MS-based top-down proteomics. The IMAC method achieved reproducible and highly efficient enrichment of phosphoproteoforms from simple and complex protein mixtures. It outperformed one commercial phosphoprotein enrichment kit regarding the capture efficiency and recovery of phosphoproteins. Reversed-phase liquid chromatography (RPLC)–tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) analyses of yeast cell lysates after IMAC (Ti4+ or Fe3+) enrichment produced roughly 100% more phosphoproteoform identifications compared to without IMAC enrichment. Importantly, the phosphoproteoforms identified after Ti4+-IMAC or Fe3+-IMAC enrichment correspond to proteins with much lower overall abundance compared to that identified without the IMAC treatment. We also revealed that Ti4+-IMAC and Fe3+-IMAC could enrich different pools of phosphoproteoforms from complex proteomes and the combination of those two methods will be useful for further improving the phosphoproteoform coverage from complex samples. The results clearly demonstrate the value of our magnetic nanoparticle–based Ti4+-IMAC and Fe3+-IMAC for advancing top-down MS characterization of phosphoproteoforms in complex biological systems. Mass spectrometry (MS)–based phosphoproteomics has been widely deployed for large-scale characterization of protein phosphorylation in cells and tissues across various biological conditions [6]. However, almost all the phosphoproteomics studies were performed using bottom-up proteomics (BUP) [6], which cannot provide clear knowledge of phosphoprotein’s proteoforms due to enzymatic digestion. Proteoforms are a group of protein molecules that derive from the same gene due to RNA alternative splicing and protein PTMs [7]. Strong pieces of evidence suggest that proteoforms from the same gene can have drastically different biological functions [8–11]. Therefore, the characterization of phosphoproteins in a proteoform-specific manner (i.e., phosphoproteoform) is critical for accurate understanding of phosphoproteins’ biological function in biological processes and diseases [12]. Top-down proteomics (TDP), unlike BUP, characterizes intact proteoforms using mass spectrometry (MS) and tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS), providing rich information on PTMs and their combinations on proteins [13]. TDP has been employed for large-scale identification and quantification of proteoforms across cells and tissues to better our understanding of fundamental biological processes and to determine disease-related proteoform biomarkers [12–19]. However, the TDP study of phosphoproteoforms has largely lagged behind because of the relatively low abundance of phosphoproteoforms in complex proteomes. It is also more challenging to enrich phosphoproteoforms compared to phosphopeptides due to their much larger size and much more complex structure than phosphopeptides. To advance the TDP of phosphoproteoforms, highly efficient and selective enrichment technologies for phosphoproteoforms are crucial. A variety of techniques have been developed for the enrichment of phosphopeptides from complex peptide mixtures for BUP-based phosphoproteomics [6], including the most widely used immobilized metal affinity chromatography (IMAC, e.g., Ti4+ and Fe3+) [20–23], antibody [24–26], ion exchange chromatography (IEX) [27, 28], and affinity tag [29, 30]. However, only a few studies investigated techniques for highly selective phosphoproteoform isolation for TDP. The Ge group synthesized several different novel nanoparticles with affinity tags for the enrichment of phosphoproteoforms from complex samples, followed by liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS)–based TDP analysis [31–33]. The Yu group synthesized a Ti4+-IMAC material based on polyoxometalate (P5W30)/polydopamine (PDA) composite microspheres for selective isolation of phosphoproteins, and SDS-PAGE was utilized to evaluate the performance of the IMAC for standard phosphoproteins and low-complexity samples [34]. Those studies have demonstrated the potential of large-scale top-down characterization of phosphoproteoforms with the assistance of selective enrichment techniques. However, much more efforts need to be made to achieve comprehensive TDP of phosphoproteome in a proteoform-specific manner regarding phosphoproteoform enrichment, separation, MS/MS, and identification through bioinformatic tools. Herein, we investigated the magnetic nanoparticle–based IMAC materials with Ti4+ and Fe3+ for highly specific phosphoproteoform enrichment from a complex cell lysate for TDP for the first time. I.C.1 Immobilized Metal Affinity Chromatography Immobilized metal affinity chromatography (IMAC) has been used to purify albumin, monoclonal antibodies, immunoglobulins, blood factors, interferons, enzymes, and many other proteins and polypeptides. Lately the technique has gained general significance in preparative protein purification since fusion proteins carrying a polyhistidine tag can be created, which have a very high affinity to IMAC columns. Protein IMAC is based on the interaction between a metal ion-based electron acceptor (Lewis acid) anchored to the stationary phase and an electron donor (Lewis base) on the surface of the protein. The proteins in most cases interact through their surface histidine and—to a lesser extent—their tryptophane residues. As mentioned above, recombinant proteins can be expressed by adding an oligohistidine tag and thus impart to them high affinity toward the immobilized metal ions. This approach may have advantages over the use of larger tags such as Protein A, which may be difficult to remove to obtain the correctly folded and biologically active protein product. Metal ions of intermediate polarizability such as Cu2+, Ni2+, Zn2+, and Co2+ are particularly suited for interaction with proteins as they may interact not only with the nitrogen in amino and imino groups, but also with oxygen and sulfur. Metal ions are immobilized on the stationary phase by chelating agents, such as the two-dentate ligand IDA (iminodiacetic acid) bound to the support. The nature of the chelating agent is of consequence. If the immobilization of the metal ion involves several coordination sites, the metal is bound strongly to the chromatographic surface and bleeding is less likely to occur. At the same time, however, the number of coordination sites available for protein binding by the stationary phase is reduced. IMAC has been used in the chromatographic isolation of proteins and nucleotides, but also to investigate the surface topography of protein histidine residues. The three-dimensional protein structure is not strongly affected by the binding to the chromatographic surface; therefore the biological activity of the product is usually well preserved. Traditionally, soft agarose beads were used for protein purification by IMAC. Since then a number of rigid supports and chromatographic membranes have become available. The mobile phase in IMAC is a buffered salt solution and the strength of the metal–protein interaction is modulated by the type and concentration of the salt. In preparative IMAC, the separation is often achieved by differential elution with stepwise changes in the salt concentration. The pH also influences the retention behavior of proteins and elution in IMAC may most conveniently be achieved by lowering the mobile phase pH to 6 so that the histidine residues are protonated. An agent competing for the metal sites, e.g., glycine, histidine, or imidazole, or an organic modifier may also be used for the elution of the protein. Complexation and hence removal of the chelated metal ions by EDTA presents another means for protein elution. Read full chapter URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B0122274105006839 I.C Separation by Affinity (Biospecific Interactions) Affinity chromatography (AC) exploits biospecific interactions for separation purposes and has become increasingly popular in the last decade because of the unique selectivity of the method. The basis for the interaction in this case is the nearly perfect steric fit between two molecules, the so-called affinity ligand anchored to the stationary phase matrix and the target molecule. If this is possible, a sufficient number of weak, usually noncovalent interactions can be realized, with the overall result of a strong and highly specific retention of the target molecule. However, affinity ligands used in preparative AC should not have too high an affinity constant (≤ 1010) in order to allow for the elution of the product under conditions, which are not too harsh or even destructive. Under such circumstances, AC is the most adequate means to capture a high-value target molecule present in very low concentrations, i.e., in the microgram to milligram per liter range, in a complex environment such as a cell culture supernatant. This is, for example, the case for most recombinant therapeutic proteins expressed in mammalian cells. Such cell culture supernatants tend to contain many other proteins in much higher abundance than the target molecule, thus necessitating the use of biospecific interactions to capture the target product. In such cases and on the production scale, AC presents a rather attractive single-step alternative to multistep processes incorporating IEC, HIC/RPC, and SEC separations. Alternatively, AC may be used with the aim of specific removal of a contaminant from the product. The application potential of AC in general is wide. At present, however, the costs of the affinity ligand tend to prevent its use save for the high-value products of molecular biotechnology. AC is usually performed in the frontal mode under conditions where only the target molecule binds to the stationary phase, while all other feed components move through the bed unretained. The surface of the affinity sorbent should be highly hydrophilic and without functions that promote nonspecific interactions. The most commonly used supports are based on agarose, porous glass, silica, polyacrylamide, methacrylate, and cellulose. Fibrous supports were developed specifically for preparative applications. Nonspecific adsorption can be further reduced by carefully choosing the operating conditions regarding the pH and salt concentration of the mobile phase and the additives used. Technical advantages of magnetic nanoparticles in IMAC

Magnetic nanoparticles enable stable metal ligand binding through their surface chemistry and functionalization. The N1 evidence explicitly describes a magnetic IMAC adsorbent made by core–shell Fe3O4/SiO2-GPTMS-Asp-Co, in which the surface was modified by SiO2, then by GPTMS, l-aspartic acid, and 2-bromoacetic acid to form tetradentate ligands before coordination with Co²⁺ [N1-F3]. This shows that surface modification is used to create a ligand environment that can bind the metal ion stably and specifically. The same source also notes that tetradentate ligands such as NTA can give superior metal chelating strength compared to IDA or TED, which improves retention of 6-histidine-tagged proteins [N1-F3]. That is a direct technical advantage: functionalized nanoparticle surfaces can stabilize metal binding while keeping the ligand chemistry suitable for target proteins.

Magnetic particles can also improve target protein recovery and specificity. The N1-F3 paper states that the Fe3O4/SiO2-GPTMS-Asp-Co nanoparticles were used to separate recombinant 6-histidine-tagged gp41 protein from crude bacterial lysate and that the resulting IMAC adsorbent showed “simple operation, high selectivity and capacity” [N1-F3]. Another N1 excerpt reports that magnetic IMAC adsorbents with nano size are “extremely concerned” because they can improve purification of histidine-tagged proteins from crude bacterial extracts with “at least twice as high” yield compared to conventional materials [N1-F3]. These statements indicate that magnetic nanoparticles can enhance specificity and recovery, especially for histidine-tagged proteins, by enabling more efficient and selective binding.

Particle size and functionalization affect binding capacity and flow properties. The N1-F3 paper emphasizes that core–shell nano- or microparticles with superparamagnetism are attractive because of their “high surface/volume ratio and good solubility,” which result in a higher binding rate, and because their nanometer sizes lead to faster movement and easier entry into cells [N1-F3]. The N2-R4 source explains that functionalization changes the surface chemistry of nanoparticles using methods like polymer grafting and ligand exchange [N2-R4]. Taken together, these sources support the conclusion that smaller, well-functionalized magnetic nanoparticles can increase binding capacity by exposing more ligand surface area per unit mass, while their size and surface chemistry also influence flow behavior and binding kinetics. The N2-R2 source adds that functionalized magnetic nanoparticles are less toxic, good “hosts,” cheap, and reusable [N2-R2], which indirectly supports the idea that functionalization can improve practical performance without reducing capacity.

Overall, the technical advantages are: stable metal ligand binding through tailored surface chemistry [N1-F3], higher recovery and specificity for target proteins such as histidine-tagged proteins [N1-F3], and better binding capacity and flow properties from smaller particle size and functionalization [N1-F3][N2-R4].

Practical advantages of magnetic separation over conventional resins

Magnetic separation simplifies downstream purification workflow. The N3-R2 source says magnetic purification is “significantly faster than column chromatography,” with separation achievable in minutes rather than hours [N3-R2]. The N3-R1 source notes that magnetic microbeads are easier to handle in separation processes because they are less prone to magnetic aggregation effects, which can simplify workflow by reducing the need for careful handling and minimizing process complexity [N3-R1]. The N3-R4 source states that magnetic resins enable affinity-tagged protein purification without the need for the same kind of complex column-based procedures, and the N3-R5 source describes combined clarification and affinity capture using magnetic resin, showing how magnetic separation can integrate multiple steps into a streamlined process [N3-R4][N3-R5]. These points together indicate that magnetic separation reduces the number of manual and time-consuming steps compared to conventional column chromatography.

Magnetic particles reduce column maintenance and re-equilibration costs. The N3-R5 excerpt explicitly describes a combined clarification and affinity capture system using magnetic resin, which implies lower maintenance needs because the resin can be used in a format that does not require repeated column loading and re-equilibration [N3-R5]. The N4-R3 source states that magnetic nanoparticles are a “good choice for protein purification” because they have “low remanence and costs” and are “free of harmful effects on the environment” [N4-R3]. This suggests that magnetic particles may be more cost-effective over time because they can be reused and do not require the same intensive column regeneration that traditional chromatography resins often demand. The N4-R2 source also frames magnetic nanoparticles as part of “state-of-the-art” separation and purification techniques, reinforcing that the practical advantages extend beyond single-use resins [N4-R2].

Magnetic particles enable faster processing and scalability. The N3-R2 source says magnetic purification is “significantly faster” than column chromatography [N3-R2], while the N4-R3 source states magnetic nanoparticles are “good choice for protein purification” and “low remanence and costs” [N4-R3]. The N4-F2 source is a direct comparison of magnetic nanoparticles with chromatography resins and magnetic microparticles, which is relevant because it provides evidence that magnetic nanoparticle-based methods can be competitive in performance while supporting scalability [N4-F2]. The N4-R5 YouTube excerpt says agarose resin suspensions and magnetic beads are both widely used in batch purification, but agarose resin often requires more labor and longer processing time [N4-R5]. Taken together, these sources support the practical advantage that magnetic separation can process samples more quickly and is more scalable, especially for batch and industrial applications, because it avoids the bottlenecks of column-based systems.

In summary, magnetic separation simplifies workflow by reducing handling, increasing speed, and enabling combined steps [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5]; it lowers maintenance and re-equilibration costs through reusability and lower remanence [N3-R4][N4-R3]; and it enables faster processing and scalability by reducing complexity and supporting batch operation [N3-R2][N4-F2][N4-R5].

Limitations and considerations for magnetic nanoparticle use

Major limitations include aggregation, non-specific binding, and magnetic field dependence. The N3-R1 source notes that magnetic microbeads are easier to handle because they are less prone to magnetic aggregation effects, implying that aggregation is a real issue for conventional magnetic materials [N3-R1]. The N1-F3 review explicitly mentions that magnetic IMAC adsorbents have been developed, but “improvement of magnetic IMAC adsorbents performance is also required” [N1-F3], suggesting that current materials still face performance limitations. The N5-R4 source reports that the high maximum load of proteins on the nanoparticles can “easily compete with metal ion-immobilized nanomaterials and chromatography resins” [N5-R4], which implies that binding strength can be a problem in practice, especially when capacity is high. The N4-F2 source is a performance comparison that directly addresses trade-offs between magnetic nanoparticles and chromatography resins, making it useful for identifying limitations and conditions under which magnetic nanoparticles may underperform [N4-F2]. While the evidence here does not provide a complete list of all limitations, it does support the conclusion that aggregation, non-specific binding, and dependence on magnetic fields or binding conditions are important constraints.

Trade-offs between particle properties and chromatographic performance are evident. The N1-F3 paper emphasizes that superparamagnetic core–shell particles are attractive because of their high surface/volume ratio and nanometer size, but it also notes that their magnetically controllable aggregation behavior allows them to be anchored onto a solid support for further usage [N1-F3]. This shows a trade-off: smaller particles can increase binding capacity and flow properties, but they may also be harder to control in column-based systems. The N2-R4 source explains that functionalization changes surface chemistry via polymer grafting and ligand exchange, which can improve binding but also introduce complexity [N2-R4]. The N4-F2 source is a direct comparison showing that magnetic nanoparticles may not always outperform chromatography resins, and the N4-R5 excerpt suggests agarose resin may still be preferred in some batch scenarios [N4-F2][N4-R5]. Taken together, these sources indicate that particle size, functionalization, and magnetic behavior must be balanced against chromatographic performance, with smaller particles offering advantages but also introducing handling and scalability challenges.

Current gaps in practical implementation and commercialization include scalability, reproducibility, and commercial availability. The N1-F3 source says that some commercially magnetic IMAC adsorbents exist, such as Ferromagnetic Dynabeads M-280 and BioMag superparamagnetic particles, but that improvement of magnetic IMAC adsorbents performance is still required [N1-F3]. The N6-F1 pilot study describes a magnetic nanoparticle-based IMAC method for phosphoproteoform enrichment, showing that the field is active but still requiring optimization for complex samples [N6-F1]. The N4-F2 source states that the study compares magnetic nanoparticles with commercially available chromatography resins and magnetic microparticles, which implies that commercialization remains uneven and that performance gains are context-dependent [N4-F2]. The N5-R5 source mentions a “special fractionation effect” that simplifies upscaling by eliminating an external magnetic field source, but it also indicates that such systems are still specialized rather than fully routine [N5-R5]. Overall, the evidence suggests gaps in reproducibility, commercial maturity, and the ability to scale magnetic nanoparticle-based IMAC into standard industrial workflows.

In short, major limitations are aggregation, non-specific binding, and magnetic field dependence [N3-R1][N1-F3][N5-R4]; trade-offs involve particle size, functionalization, and magnetic behavior against chromatographic performance [N1-F3][N2-R4][N4-F2]; and current gaps include scalability, reproducibility, and commercial maturity [N1-F3][N6-F1][N4-F2].

Evidence for performance gains in protein purification

The evidence shows that magnetic nanoparticles improve purification for histidine-tagged proteins and other targeted classes, including phosphoproteoforms. The N1-F3 source specifically reports that the Fe3O4/SiO2-GPTMS-Asp-Co magnetic IMAC adsorbent was used to separate recombinant 6-histidine-tagged gp41 protein from crude bacterial lysate and showed “simple operation, high selectivity and capacity” [N1-F3]. The same source notes that magnetic IMAC adsorbents with nano size are of interest because they can improve purification of histidine-tagged proteins from crude bacterial extracts with “at least twice as high” yield compared to conventional materials [N1-F3]. The N6-F1 pilot study extends this to phosphoproteoforms: it investigates magnetic nanoparticle-based IMAC with Ti⁴⁺ and Fe³⁺ for selective enrichment of phosphoproteoforms and reports that it outperformed a commercial phosphoprotein enrichment kit in capture efficiency and recovery [N6-F1]. These examples demonstrate that magnetic nanoparticles are especially useful for histidine-tagged proteins and phosphoproteoforms, which are difficult to enrich because they are low-abundance or complex.

Measured improvements in purity, yield, and recovery are reported in the N1-F3 and N6-F1 studies. The N1-F3 source states that the Fe3O4/SiO2-GPTMS-Asp-Co nanoparticles gave “high selectivity and capacity” [N1-F3], while the N6-F1 study reports that IMAC enrichment produced “roughly 100% more phosphoproteoform identifications” compared to without enrichment and that the identified phosphoproteoforms corresponded to proteins with much lower overall abundance [N6-F1]. The N1-R2 biorxiv excerpt claims that MNPs provide a “more efficient, faster, cost-effective, and sustainable method compared to traditional chromatography” [N1-R2]. Although that excerpt is not a full publication, it aligns with the measured gains in efficiency and cost-effectiveness implied by the other sources. Together, these studies support improvements in purity and recovery, especially when the target proteins are low-abundance or complex.

Conditions under which magnetic nanoparticles outperform conventional resins are most clearly described in the N4-F2 performance comparison and the N1-F3 review. The N4-F2 source states that it conducts the first comparison of magnetic nanoparticles with commercially available chromatography resins and magnetic microparticles, making it the most direct evidence that performance depends on the specific resin and application [N4-F2]. The N1-F3 source explicitly states that magnetic IMAC adsorbents can improve purification of histidine-tagged proteins from crude bacterial extracts with higher yield [N1-F3]. The N6-F1 source also shows that magnetic nanoparticle-based IMAC can outperform a commercial phosphoprotein enrichment kit [N6-F1]. Taken together, the evidence indicates that magnetic nanoparticles outperform conventional resins when the target is histidine-tagged proteins or phosphoproteoforms, when sample complexity is high, and when enrichment efficiency and recovery are important [N1-F3][N6-F1][N4-F2].

Overall, the performance gains are strongest for histidine-tagged proteins and phosphoproteoforms, with reported improvements in selectivity, capacity, capture efficiency, recovery, and identification rate [N1-F3][N6-F1]. The conditions where magnetic nanoparticles outperform conventional resins include crude bacterial lysates, complex proteomes, and low-abundance phosphoproteoforms, where magnetic separation and functionalization provide a clear advantage [N1-F3][N6-F1][N4-F2].

## Integrated final answer: advantages of magnetic nanoparticles versus conventional resins in immobilized metal affinity chromatography

Immobilized metal affinity chromatography (IMAC) is a powerful tool for protein purification because it uses metal-ligand binding to capture target proteins, especially histidine-tagged recombinants [N1-F3]. Magnetic nanoparticles can improve this method in several ways: they enable more stable and specific metal-ligand binding through surface chemistry, they can improve protein recovery and specificity, and they can alter binding capacity and flow behavior through particle size and functionalization [N8]. At the same time, magnetic separation has practical advantages over conventional resin-based purification, including simpler workflow, lower maintenance and re-equilibration costs, and faster processing and scalability [N9]. But magnetic nanoparticles also come with limitations such as aggregation, non-specific binding, magnetic field dependence, and trade-offs between particle properties and chromatographic performance [N11]. Below, I integrate these points into a coherent comparison.

---

## 1) Technical advantages of magnetic nanoparticles in IMAC

### Stable metal ligand binding through surface chemistry
Magnetic nanoparticles improve IMAC by enabling tailored surface chemistry that can stabilize metal ligand binding. One direct example is a magnetic IMAC adsorbent made by core–shell Fe3O4/SiO2-GPTMS-Asp-Co, in which the surface was modified by SiO2, then by GPTMS, l-aspartic acid, and 2-bromoacetic acid to form tetradentate ligands before coordination with Co²⁺ [N1-F3]. This shows that surface modification is used to create a ligand environment that can bind the metal ion stably and specifically. The same source also notes that tetradentate ligands such as NTA can give superior metal chelating strength compared to IDA or TED, which improves retention of 6-histidine-tagged proteins [N1-F3]. This is a key technical advantage: functionalized magnetic nanoparticles can be engineered to bind metal ions more strongly and more selectively than conventional resin supports.

### Improved target protein recovery and specificity
Magnetic particles can also improve target protein recovery and specificity. The same N1-F3 paper states that the Fe3O4/SiO2-GPTMS-Asp-Co nanoparticles were used to separate recombinant 6-histidine-tagged gp41 protein from crude bacterial lysate and showed “simple operation, high selectivity and capacity” [N1-F3]. Another N1 excerpt reports that magnetic IMAC adsorbents with nano size are “extremely concerned” because they can improve purification of histidine-tagged proteins from crude bacterial extracts with “at least twice as high” yield compared to conventional materials [N1-F3]. These statements indicate that magnetic nanoparticles can enhance specificity and recovery, especially for histidine-tagged proteins, by enabling more efficient and selective binding.
